noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand how temperature changes can affect enzyme function, including changes to the shape of active site

primer.text: Temperature is the factor that changes enzyme activity in two opposite directions. Warming towards the optimum adds kinetic energy and speeds reactions; overheating destroys the bonds holding the enzyme's shape and denatures it. This note separates those two effects so you can explain the classic temperature graph mark by mark.

lessons.title: Optimum temperature, kinetic energy and denaturation
lessons.opening: Every enzyme works fastest at its optimum temperature — 37 degrees Celsius in the human body. Below it, molecules move slowly and reactions crawl; above it, heat breaks the bonds holding the enzyme's shape and the active site is lost for good. Cold slows enzymes but never denatures them, which is exactly the contrast examiners test.
keyPoints: Each enzyme has an optimum temperature at which it works fastest; the human body's is 37 degrees Celsius.
Warming towards the optimum adds kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate collide more often.
Beyond the optimum, heat breaks the bonds holding the protein's shape and the enzyme denatures.
Denaturation is irreversible, and denatured active sites no longer fit their substrates.
Low temperatures do not denature enzymes; they only slow the reaction down.

low.restatement: Warm to the optimum and the reaction speeds up; overheat and the enzyme denatures permanently. Cold merely slows it.
low.analogy: An enzyme is like a singer: a warmer room loosens the voice, but a fire melts the instrument — and melted instruments never play again.
low.examPointer: The graph has a peak at 37 and a collapse after it; answers must name BOTH the kinetic-energy rise and the denaturation fall.

medium.restatement: The rate curve rises because collision frequency grows with kinetic energy, then falls steeply because bond breakage reshapes the active site; the two mechanisms act on opposite sides of the peak.
medium.analogy: Below the peak you are pushing a swing gently (more pushes, faster); above it you snap the swing's chains (no pushes can help).
medium.examPointer: Say 'irreversible' when defining denaturation — one word, one mark, routinely missed.

check.stem: What is the optimum temperature for enzymes in the human body?

options.text: 37 degrees Celsius
options.explanation: The note gives 37 as the human optimum.

options.text: 0 degrees Celsius
options.explanation: That is freezing, far below any working optimum.

options.text: 100 degrees Celsius
options.explanation: That would denature every enzyme long before.

options.text: 72 degrees Celsius
options.explanation: Far above the human optimum.

check.stem: Why does enzyme activity rise as temperature climbs towards the optimum?

options.text: Because denaturation speeds the reaction
options.explanation: Denaturation stops activity.

options.text: Molecules gain kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate collide more often
options.explanation: Kinetic energy and collisions explain the rise.

options.text: Because enzymes grow extra active sites when warm
options.explanation: No new sites appear.

options.text: Because substrates melt into smaller pieces
options.explanation: Substrates do not melt.

check.stem: What happens to an enzyme heated well beyond its optimum?

options.text: It returns to normal when cooled
options.explanation: Denaturation is irreversible.

options.text: It breaks into amino acids immediately
options.explanation: The protein denatures; full digestion is not claimed.

options.text: Its bonds break, the shape is lost, and substrates no longer fit the active site
options.explanation: This is the full denaturation account.

options.text: It works faster because it is warmer
options.explanation: Activity stops rather than rises.

check.stem: Which statement about LOW temperatures is correct?

options.text: Cold denatures enzymes permanently
options.explanation: Heat beyond optimum denatures, not cold.

options.text: Cold raises the optimum temperature
options.explanation: The optimum stays put.

options.text: Cold breaks the bonds holding the shape
options.explanation: Bond breakage is the overheating story.

options.text: Enzymes are not denatured; they simply work more slowly
options.explanation: Cold slows rather than destroys.

check.stem: Why is denaturation described as irreversible?

options.text: Because once the shape is lost it cannot be regained, so activity stops for good
options.explanation: The note states denatured enzymes never regain proper shape.

options.text: Because cooling slowly restores the original bonds
options.explanation: Nothing restores them.

options.text: Because the substrate fills the site permanently
options.explanation: Substrates no longer fit at all.

options.text: Because the enzyme dissolves into the solution
options.explanation: Dissolving is not the mechanism.

check.stem: State the term for the permanent loss of an enzyme's working shape caused by overheating.
Name the bonds whose breakage causes denaturation.
check.modelAnswer: The bonds that hold the enzyme's protein shape in place.

check.stem: Explain why the rate of an enzyme reaction climbs, peaks and then collapses as temperature rises from cold to far above the optimum.
check.modelAnswer: From cold towards the optimum, added kinetic energy makes enzyme and substrate collide more often, so the rate climbs; at the peak the site still fits; beyond it, heat breaks the shape-holding bonds, the active site no longer complements the substrate, and the rate collapses irreversibly.

check.stem: Food is frozen to preserve it. Using enzyme theory, explain why freezing slows spoilage rather than stopping it outright.
check.modelAnswer: Freezing removes kinetic energy, so the spoilage enzymes' reactions run very slowly — no denaturation occurs, which is why spoilage resumes slowly once food warms again rather than having been destroyed.

glossary.definition: The temperature at which an enzyme works fastest.
The irreversible loss of an enzyme's shape when heat breaks the bonds holding it, destroying active-site fit.
The energy of molecular movement, which grows as temperature rises.
